title: Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019
short_title: Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would tighten rules on unions and employer groups after a royal commission found misconduct.
It would let the Federal Court ban officials from office and cancel an organisation's registration for serious breaches.
New rules would also block a merger that is not in the public interest.
changes: Include serious criminal offences as a ground for automatic disqualification from office.
Empower the Federal Court to disqualify officials who repeatedly break industrial laws or are not fit and proper.
Create an offence for a disqualified person to still act as an official.
Allow the Federal Court to cancel registration for unlawful conduct or serious criminal offences.
Expand the Federal Court's power to appoint an administrator to fix governance problems.
Introduce a public interest test for amalgamations, considering each organisation's compliance record among other things.
summary.affected: Registered employee and employer organisations and their officials.

divisions.question: The majority voted against a motion introduced by Watson MP [Tony Burke](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/watson/tony_burke) (Labor), which means it failed. Had this motion succeeded, the bill would have been rejected. ### Motion text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"the House:* > > *(1) declines to give the bill a [second reading](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html); and* > > *(2) notes that:* > >> *(a) this Government has not proposed legislation to deal with important workplace relations matters, such as wage theft, flat lining wages growth, or deaths in the workplace;* >> >> *(b) this bill and the Act it seeks to amend represent an inconsistent approach by the Government to responding to Royal Commissions; and* >> >> *(c) the Government's entire approach to workplace relations laws is to attack workers' organisations with the specific intention of weakening the capacity of those organisations to combat wage theft, achieve wage growth, and ensure that workplaces are safe".*

The majority voted in favour of a motion to agree with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss it in greater detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was [introduced in order to](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6348): * *include certain serious criminal offences as a new category of ‘prescribed offence’ for the purposes of the automatic disqualification regime in relation to registered organisations;* * *establish an offence for a disqualified person to continue to act as an official or in a way that influences the affairs of an organisation;* * *allow the Federal Court to disqualify officials from holding office in certain circumstances or if they are otherwise not a fit and proper person;* * *allow the Federal Court to cancel the registration of an organisation on a range of grounds;* * *expand the grounds on which the Federal Court may order remedial action to deal with governance issues in an organisation;* * *expressly provide that the Federal Court may appoint an administrator to an organisation or part of an organisation as part of a remedial scheme;* * *introduce a public interest test for amalgamations of registered organisations; and* * *make minor and technical amendments.*

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to reject the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it attacks unions instead of addressing wage theft, stagnant wages (growing eight times slower than profits), and over 200 workplace deaths per year, and that its provisions—allowing any person of sufficient interest to disqualify officials or deregister unions—would be weaponised by employers like Liberal donor Gerry Hanssen.

speeches.speaker: Lucy Wicks
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would expand grounds for disqualifying union officials and make it a criminal offence for disqualified persons to hold office. The speaker cited the CFMMEU as having been fined over $16 million, with over 2,000 breaches and 74 representatives before the courts, and described alleged union intimidation and thuggery, including the physical assault of a volunteer.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government is not anti-union but opposes unions that break the law, specifically targeting the CFMMEU for over 2,000 incidents of law-breaking and $16 million in fines. He supported the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would make it easier for the Federal Court to deregister organisations like the CFMMEU and disqualify officials convicted of serious offences or repeated industrial law breaches.

speeches.speaker: Milton Dick
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is an attack on unions and workers, violating human rights and international law, and would further suppress wages—citing a 50‑year low in workers’ share of income, penalty rate cuts costing some workers up to $26,000, and total losses of $2.9 billion.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it is an obsessive government attack on unions that would suppress wages, violate international labour rights, and undermine democratic representation. They noted the bill goes beyond the Heydon royal commission recommendations, is largely unchanged from a 2017 version, and contrasts with the government's failure to establish a national anticorruption commission.

speeches.speaker: Nicolle Flint
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is needed to tackle illegal behaviour by unions and employer organisations, citing CFMMEU official John Setka’s 59 convictions and union intimidation during the Boothby election campaign. The bill would give courts greater powers to disqualify officials, cancel registrations, and enforce accountability for law-breaking organisations.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it allows employers or others to deregister unions and disqualify officials via a fit-and-proper-person test. He cited the government's $45 million royal commission into unions as a political attack, defended unions' role in securing wages and conditions, and referenced the Health Services Union's industrial dispute over hospital safety and ACTU president Michele O'Neil's opposition to the bill.

speeches.speaker: Patrick Gorman
speeches.brief: Wage theft is compared to robbery, with examples including Michael Hill's estimated $25 million in underpayments and 7-Eleven's "slavery-like" conditions; the speaker criticises the government for prioritising the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 over addressing wage theft and worker exploitation.

speeches.speaker: Ged Kearney
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is a union-bashing bill that would allow employers and interested parties to seek deregistration of unions, citing examples like the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation's past industrial action for nurse-patient ratios in Victoria and potential applications by figures like Gerry Hanssen or George Calombaris. The speaker also highlighted wage theft, exploitation of migrant farmworkers earning as little as $4.80 per hour, and stagnant wages, while criticising the government for not targeting corporate misconduct or the banking sector.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 was argued to enforce the rule of law in the workplace by penalising unlawful conduct by unions and employer groups. The speaker cited findings from the Heydon royal commission, including abuse of right-of-entry, coercion, extortion and blackmail, and claimed that unlawful industrial action increases infrastructure costs by 30–78% compared to other countries, with the CFMMEU accumulating $16.4 million in fines since 2004. The bill introduces automatic disqualification from office for officials convicted of offences carrying a five-year prison term, expands court powers to disqualify unfit officers, allows the Fair Work Commission to apply a public interest test to union mergers, and enables court-appointed administrators for dysfunctional organisations.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: The member argued that the Liberal Party lectures unions on integrity while facing its own issues, citing the member for Hume under investigation for alleged illegal poisoning of grasslands and record water payments linked to a Cayman Islands entity.

speeches.speaker: Tim Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, stating that the people of Goldstein expect union representatives to be law-abiding. They criticised the opposition's post-election behaviour, describing it as following the seven stages of grief, and referenced the opposition's shifting stance on $387 billion in tax cuts.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: Centre Alliance gave qualified support to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 but raised concerns about the ministerial power to deregister unions, arguing safeguards are needed to prevent political exploitation, and noted that unions are not the only organisations requiring legislative accountability.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is a broken promise and an attack on unions, not the Commonwealth Integrity Commission legislation promised by Prime Minister Morrison. They listed Labor’s alternative policies—including a tradie pay guarantee, a $7 million litigation fund, director identification numbers, increased penalties for phoenix activity, and naming and shaming tax offenders—and noted that median household income fell by almost $500 in 2017 according to the HILDA Survey.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, citing the death of German backpacker Marianka Heumann in a Perth construction site fall and the subsequent exclusion of CFMEU organisers by Liberal Party donor Gerry Hanssen, who was fined $62,000. He argued the bill is an anti-union obsession that ignores employer misconduct, wage theft, and stagnant wages, and defended his position on John Setka as respecting unions' democratic independence.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is an unjustified attack on unions, citing 190 annual workplace deaths, the Ark Tribe case, and widespread business exploitation, and claimed the bill allows disqualification for minor technical breaches, prevents amalgamations, and goes beyond the Heydon royal commission's recommendations.

speeches.speaker: Brian Mitchell
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it unfairly targets unions and will harm workers, citing that unionised workplaces pay men 12% more and women 18% more, and that one-third of employers underpay superannuation entitlements by $3.5 billion annually. They criticised the government for not pursuing wage theft or bank misconduct with similar harshness, referencing Liberal Party member Gerry Hanssen’s “blind hatred” of unions and the bill’s association with Peter Reith and John Howard.

speeches.speaker: Bob Katter
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the CFMMEU is the only organisation fighting against the import of overseas workers that undermines Australian pay and conditions, citing that one in every two new jobs created since 2013 has gone to a temporary visa holder. He also recounted his personal experience of dangerous work conditions at Mount Isa Mines and a union that sided with bosses, leading him to join the CFMEU.
